questions.q: The task list got slow. The team suggests Redis, more servers, a bigger database and a rewrite. What should happen first?
questions.explain: Each guess costs days and may miss the cause entirely. A measurement tells you whether the time is CPU, I/O or queueing, and which function or query is responsible.
options: Add Redis, because caching helps almost every read
Add servers, because it is the fastest change to deploy
Measure where the time goes (load test, event-loop delay, profile), then change one thing and measure again

questions.q: During busy hours the task list is slow, and so is /health, which does no work. What does that suggest?
questions.explain: All routes share one event loop. A route that does nothing only slows down when the loop itself is busy, which points at CPU work in the process, not at a dependency.
options: Something is keeping the event loop busy, so every request waits for its turn on the CPU
The health check has a bug

questions.q: Only POST /tasks is slow. Event-loop delay is 2 ms, database CPU is 10%, and 30 requests are waiting for a pool connection. What kind of slowness is this?
questions.explain: Both the loop and the database are nearly idle, yet requests wait. They are queueing for a limited resource. Find out how long each connection is held before touching the pool size.
options: Queueing: something holds connections too long, for example a transaction left open during another call

questions.q: A load test of the generated project reports 300 2xx responses, 1700 non 2xx responses. What should you conclude?
questions.explain: The generated project limits each client to 300 requests per minute, and a load tester is one client. Read the status counts before any latency number, and use a load-test configuration with a higher limit.
options: Most requests were refused with 429 by the rate limiter, so the latency numbers describe the limiter, not the route
The database ran out of connections
autocannon is misconfigured and the numbers can be ignored

questions.q: Why run the load generator in a separate process from the server when you want real numbers?
questions.explain: In one process, the client's parsing and bookkeeping compete with the server for the same loop. That is acceptable for comparing two routes, not for absolute numbers.
options: Because fetch does not work inside a server process
The client's own work also runs on the event loop, so it slows the server it is measuring
Because Node.js allows only one HTTP connection per process

questions.q: In a CPU profile, what is a function's self time?
questions.explain: Total time includes callees; self time does not. The functions with the most self time are where the CPU actually is, which makes them the place to look first.
options: The time from its first call to its last call
The time spent in the function's own code, not counting the functions it calls
The time it spent waiting for I/O
The time since the process started

questions.q: The profile's top entry is json http.js:4, the project's helper that builds JSON responses, not JSON.stringify itself. Why?
questions.explain: Native built-ins usually do not appear as separate entries, so their cost shows up in the caller. The helper is where 10,000 tasks were turned into text on every request.
options: The helper has a bug that makes it slow
JSON.stringify is a built-in, and its time is counted in the JavaScript function that called it
The profiler cannot measure built-ins at all, so that time is lost
Because the file is compiled from TypeScript

questions.q: After paginating the list, the rate limiter's check tops the profile of the load test, which used RATE_LIMIT_MAX=1000000 from one client. With the production limit of 300 it drops to about 3%. What is the right conclusion?
questions.explain: A sliding-log limiter costs time proportional to the requests one client made in the window. In production each client stays under 300; the test made one client send everything under a limit of a million.
options: Remove the rate limiter, it is too slow
The hot spot came from the test setup; load tests should use production-like settings and many client addresses
Rate limiting always costs a fifth of the CPU
The pagination fix made the limiter slower

questions.q: Nine requests take about 15 ms and one takes 900 ms. Which number best shows what the slowest users feel?
questions.explain: The mean (about 100 ms here) describes nobody, and the median hides the slow tail completely. High percentiles show the tail that alerts should watch.
options: A high percentile such as p95 or p99

questions.q: Why does an N+1 query pattern often look harmless in development?
questions.explain: The problem is the number of round trips, which grows with the page. Count queries per request in development and tests instead of judging by feel.
options: Development databases do not support joins
With little data and a local database each query is very fast, so 51 queries still feel instant; in production each one pays a network round trip and a pool checkout
ORMs remove N+1 queries automatically in development

questions.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Index Scan using tasks_pkey … (actual rows=50) with Filter: (owner_id = 'u-42') and Rows Removed by Filter: 24492. What does it tell you?
questions.explain: Compare rows read with rows returned. The filter threw away tens of thousands of other users' rows. A composite index that matches the filter and the order makes the work proportional to the page.
options: The query is optimal: it returned only 50 rows
It read about 24,500 rows to return 50; an index on (owner_id, id) would let it read only the rows it returns

questions.q: Page 801 with LIMIT 50 OFFSET 40000 shows actual rows=40050 on the index scan. What is the better query for deep pages?
questions.explain: OFFSET makes the database produce and discard every earlier row. A keyset query starts right after the last row the client saw, so every page reads 50 rows.
options: A keyset cursor: WHERE id > $lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 50
Fetching all rows and slicing in JavaScript

questions.q: With a pool of 40, nobody waits in the pool, but the slowest query now takes 200 ms instead of 20 ms and the total time did not improve. What happened?
questions.explain: Past the database's capacity, more connections only make each query slower. The pool's waiting count looks healthy while the real queue hides in the database, where it also slows other services.
options: The queue moved from the pool into the database, whose 4 cores now split time among 40 queries
Bigger pools always make individual queries faster

questions.q: Little's law says the board route needs about 102 busy connections at 400 requests a second, because it makes 51 queries per request. What is the right response?
questions.explain: Pool trouble is often a query problem in disguise. Fewer round trips per request shrink the number of connections needed directly.
options: Raise the pool to 110 connections per process
Fix the N+1 query so the route makes 1 or 2 queries, which needs about 2 connections

questions.q: Why is one very popular key a problem in a shared cache such as a Redis cluster, when it is harmless in a single process?
questions.explain: A key lives on one node. Concentrated traffic overloads that node while others idle, and a synchronized expiry makes every server reload at once.
options: Every request from every app server goes to the one node that owns the key, so that node saturates, and all servers miss together when it expires
It is not a problem in a shared cache either

questions.q: A local in-process cache with a 1-second TTL sits in front of the shared cache for the launch-week board. For which data would that layer be a bad idea?
questions.explain: The local layer can serve a value up to one second old in each process. For a balance that decides a payment, stale is wrong; read it from the source inside the transaction.
options: A board's list of task titles
Feature flag values that change a few times a day
A customer's wallet balance used to approve a ₦50,000 transfer

questions.q: Why add jitter to the TTL of cache entries that are written at the same time?
questions.explain: Entries written together would otherwise expire together, sending a wave of misses to the database. A small, per-key offset spreads the reloads out.
options: So they do not all expire in the same moment and cause a burst of reloads

questions.q: A mail provider allows 5 connections and each email takes 40 ms. You raise the worker's concurrency from 5 to 20. What happens?
questions.explain: By Little's law, 5 connections ÷ 0.04 s = 125 per second, whatever the concurrency. Set concurrency at the knee, where the downstream limit is reached.
options: Throughput stays at about 125 emails a second; the extra jobs wait at the provider, holding memory and connections
The provider allows more connections automatically

questions.q: Which queue metric tells you most directly that workers are falling behind?
questions.explain: A deep queue that drains quickly is fine. An old job means work is waiting longer than it should, whatever the depth.
options: The total number of jobs ever processed
The age of the oldest waiting job

questions.q: A service keeps recentQuotes.set(requestId, quote) in a module-level Map and never deletes. What will you see in production?
questions.explain: The map keeps every quote reachable, keyed by something unbounded. Every in-memory structure needs a bound, such as a cache's maxEntries.
options: Nothing, the garbage collector frees it
Heap growth with traffic, longer garbage collection pauses, and eventually an out-of-memory restart

questions.q: Why assert "one query per page" and "a page is at most 8 KB" instead of "responds within 50 ms" in unit tests?
questions.explain: Time-based assertions flake on a busy machine and pass on a fast one. A new query per item or a missing limit changes the count every time.
options: Counts and sizes are exact and do not depend on how fast the CI machine is, and they catch the causes of slowness
Milliseconds cannot be measured in tests
50 ms is too strict for any API

questions.q: A middleware parses every response body and writes it into a log line. What is its cost, compared to one that logs status, size and duration?
questions.explain: Parsing and serializing the body again multiplies the work of producing it. Log facts about the response, not the response.
options: The same, because logging is asynchronous
Proportional to the body size on every request; for large bodies it can cost more than the handler
Zero, because the body is already a string
Lower, because it avoids a second log line

questions.q: createTimingMiddleware() adds a Server-Timing header. What is the concern on a public API?
questions.explain: Timing information can leak facts, such as whether a record was already cached. Send it to internal clients, or sample it.
options: Timings help an outsider tell cached from uncached answers, and similar timing differences

questions.q: An idle process with monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 }) reports a p50 of about 20 ms. Why?
questions.explain: The value is the time from one sample to the next. An idle loop at a 20 ms resolution reports about 20 ms; only the part above the resolution is lateness.
options: The histogram records the time between samples, which includes the 20 ms interval itself; subtract it to get the delay
Node adds 20 ms to every timer

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: One 900 ms request pulls the mean to 102.2, which describes no request. The nearest-rank p95 of 10 values is the 10th value, the slow one; the median is the 5th, 14.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Busy slots = arrival rate × time each. 400 × 0.005 = 2; 51 queries per request multiplies the rate; 125 emails a second at 40 ms keep 5 connections busy; 50 jobs a second that take 2 s each need 100 slots.
questions.code:
const busy = (perSecond, secondsEach) => Math.ceil(perSecond * secondsEach);

console.log(busy(400, 0.005), busy(400 * 51, 0.005), busy(125, 0.04), busy(50, 2));

questions.q: A lag monitor samples every 10 ms. What does this print?
questions.explain: The recorded values include the 10 ms sampling interval. 10.3 ms rounds to 10, minus 10 is 0; 9.2 rounds to 9, and Math.max keeps it at 0; 479 ms means the loop was 469 ms late.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: One query for the list plus one per task is 1 + 3 = 4. The batched version makes one list query and one query for the deduplicated ids, however many tasks there are.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each page starts after the last id of the previous page. A short page means there is nothing more, so next is undefined and the loop stops.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each task is about 30 bytes of JSON, so the size grows with the number of items: about 30 KB for 1,000 and 1.5 KB for a page of 50. Even an empty page has its wrapper, {"items":[],"next":-1}, 22 bytes. Serialization time grows the same way, which is why a hard page limit matters.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first read of each key is a miss that loads and stores it; hot-key tracking counts hits. board.launch was read four times: one miss, then 3 hits. Six reads, three hits: a hit rate of 0.5.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Concurrent misses for the same key wait for the one load in flight instead of starting their own, so the database is asked once. The request after that finds the stored value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The map grows with every request; the cache evicts to stay at maxEntries. Keyed by request id, the map is a slow leak.

questions.q: This TTL jitter uses a simple sum of character codes as its hash. What does it print?
questions.explain: 97 + 98 = 195, and 195 % 100 = 95, so both keys get 60,000 + 95 × 60 = 65,700 ms. The same key always gets the same TTL, which is good, but a sum ignores the order of the characters, so keys made of the same letters collide. The lesson's FNV-1a hash mixes the order in, spreading such keys apart.

questions.q: Eight queries arrive at once at a pool of 3 connections. What does this print?
questions.explain: Three queries take the free connections; the other five wait, all at the same moment. Each finished query hands its connection to the next waiter, and when nobody waits the connection goes back, so all 3 are free at the end.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Concurrency caps how many jobs run at the same time; all ten still finish. Throughput then depends on how long each job takes and what it waits for.

questions.q: A sliding-log limiter copies a client's timestamp list on every check. What does this print?
questions.explain: With a max of 3, the list stops at 3 entries: 0+1+2+3+3+3 = 12 copies. With a high max it keeps growing: 0+1+2+3+4+5 = 15, and in general about n²/2 for n checks. That is why a huge limit made the limiter a hot spot.

questions.q: Write percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank method: sort a copy ascending and return the value at position ceil(p / 100 × n), counting from 1. Return undefined for an empty list. Do not change the input array.
questions.explain: Sort with a numeric comparator (the default sort compares strings, putting 120 before 14), and sort a copy so the caller's data stays in order. Real monitoring systems estimate percentiles from histograms, but the idea is the same.

questions.q: Write poolSize({ requestsPerSecond, queriesPerRequest, queryMs, processes }) that returns the connections needed per process by Little's law, rounded up, plus 50% headroom (also rounded up), with a minimum of 2.
questions.explain: 400 × 2 × 0.005 = 4 busy connections over 4 processes is 1 each, 2 with headroom. The N+1 version needs 102 in total, about 26 per process and 39 with headroom: across 4 processes that is more than PostgreSQL's default 100. The number tells you to fix the queries first.

questions.q: Write withQueryCount(db). It returns { db, count }: a wrapped object whose query(sql, params) calls the original and increments a counter, and a function count() that returns how many queries were made. Use it to show that loadBoard makes 4 queries.
questions.explain: Wrapping the one function every query goes through gives a count without changing any repository code. In a test, assert the count; in development, log it per request.

questions.q: Write listPage(tasks, { limit = 50, after }) for tasks sorted by id. Refuse a limit that is not a whole number from 1 to 100 by returning { error: "limit must be 1-100" }. Otherwise return { items, next }, where next is the last id when the page is full, and undefined otherwise.
questions.explain: JSON.stringify leaves out a property whose value is undefined, so the last page has no next. The hard maximum is what keeps one request from asking for everything again.

questions.q: Write hotKeys(log, n) that returns the n most frequent keys as "key count" strings, most frequent first, ties in alphabetical order.
questions.explain: Count with a Map, then sort by count and break ties by name so the output is stable. A key with a large share of all reads is a candidate for a local cache layer.

questions.q: Write checkBudget(name, measured, budget) that prints one line per budget key, PASS or FAIL, in the form PASS GET /tasks queries 2 <= 2, and returns true only if every measured value is within its budget.
questions.explain: Report every budget, not just the first failure, so one run shows everything that regressed. Budgets on counts and bytes are exact, so they never flake on a slow machine.
questions.expected:
PASS  GET /tasks queries 2 <= 2
PASS  GET /tasks bytes 7157 <= 8192
FAIL  GET /board queries 51 <= 2
PASS  GET /board bytes 5200 <= 8192
true false

questions.q: Write createBoundedMap(max) with get(key), set(key, value) and size(). When a set would exceed max, remove the least recently used key; a get counts as a use.
questions.explain: A Map iterates in insertion order, so re-inserting a key on every use keeps the least recently used key first. Reading rice saved it; beans was the oldest and was evicted. The memory used is now bounded by max, whatever the traffic.
